The investigation evaluated hospital records between January 2023 and June 2024 to address the lack of large comparative cohorts evaluating dengue severity in individuals with compromised immune defenses. The study included 894 patients diagnosed with dengue, of whom 59 met specific clinical criteria for immunocompromised status. Qualifying conditions included living with HIV with CD4 counts below 350 cells per microliter, having received a solid organ transplant or a hematopoietic stem cell transplant within the preceding two years, active malignancy, asplenia or splenectomy, and medical regimens requiring immunosuppressive medications. Demographic analysis revealed that immunocompromised patients were significantly older, presenting with a median age of 47.0 years compared to 33.5 years in the non-immunocompromised group. Additionally, these patients carried a higher baseline burden of preexisting health conditions, reflected in a median Charlson comorbidity index of 1 versus 0 among non-immunocompromised individuals. While primary clinical features at initial presentation were largely similar, an absence of fever was noted more frequently in the immunocompromised cohort, occurring in 10.2 percent compared to 1.1 percent. Routine laboratory values appeared comparable upon admission, yet immunocompromised patients subsequently exhibited significantly lower nadir platelet counts and prolonged thrombocytopenia throughout their illness. Primary clinical endpoints showed marked disparities, with severe dengue according to World Health Organization 2009 criteria documented in 22 percent of immunocompromised individuals compared to only 4.9 percent of non-immunocompromised patients. Patients with impaired immunity also experienced higher rates of hospital admission, longer stays, and increased 30-day mortality. In multivariable analysis, immunocompromised status and comorbidity index were both independently associated with severe dengue, yielding an odds ratio of 3.43 for immune impairment and 1.33 for the comorbidity score. The researchers concluded that these findings provide critical evidence demonstrating an elevated risk of severe outcomes, highlighting the urgent need for improved strategies for prevention and clinical management in this population. Dengue virus, an enveloped pathogen belonging to the Flaviviridae family, is transmitted to humans through the bites of infected female Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes. Globally, dengue represents an escalating public health crisis across tropical and subtropical territories, including South-east Asia, Latin America, the Pacific Islands, and the Caribbean. Epidemiological assessments recorded by the World Health Organization report that over 390 million people contract dengue annually, resulting in roughly 22,000 fatal outcomes, with the Asian continent bearing approximately 67 percent of all clinical cases. Despite the clinical spectrum ranging from sudden high fever, retro-orbital eye pain, arthralgia, headache, and severe myalgia to life-threatening conditions such as dengue hemorrhagic fever and dengue shock syndrome, no targeted antiviral pharmaceuticals are currently approved for clinical therapy. Supportive treatment relies almost entirely on careful fluid balance management to mitigate severe dehydration. To overcome the current therapeutic deficit, investigators have increasingly focused on plant-derived secondary metabolites that display broad-spectrum antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and antiviral characteristics. The structural architecture of the dengue virion features an approximately eleven-kilobase single-stranded positive-sense RNA genome that encodes three structural proteins comprising the capsid, membrane, and envelope proteins, along with seven non-structural proteins designated NS1, NS2A, NS2B, NS3, NS4A, NS4B, and NS5. Among these, the surface-exposed envelope glycoprotein plays an indispensable role in mediating infection by facilitating virion attachment to host cell surface receptors and driving subsequent membrane fusion. Structurally, the envelope monomer is organized into three distinct structural units: domain I, which acts as a central hinge orchestrating conformational shifts; domain II, which contains a highly conserved hydrophobic fusion loop responsible for dimerization and host membrane insertion; and domain III, which functions as the primary receptor-binding domain. Because the envelope protein also mediates viral hemagglutination and neutralizes host immunological defenses, disrupting its structural integrity represents a strategic approach for halting infection. The research team devised an integrated in silico screening pipeline that began with the systematic collection of dengue virus envelope protein sequences deposited in the UniProt database across four antigenically distinct serotypes, designated DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4. Their sequence retrieval yielded eighteen distinct strains for DENV-1, eleven for DENV-2, five for DENV-3, and eight for DENV-4, representing viral isolates collected over multiple decades from Asia, South America, North America, and Australia. The polypeptide chains displayed an average length of 488 plus or minus 8.09 amino acid residues. To pinpoint structurally conserved target domains across serotypes, the investigators conducted multiple sequence alignment using the ClustalW program within the Clustal Omega suite. Based on previous structural literature, six specific functional pockets and active site ranges were mapped along the envelope sequence: amino acid residues 45 to 65, 110 to 140, 190 to 225, 255 to 290, 300 to 345, and 346 to 390, confirming homologous binding regions shared among diverse geographic variants. Three-dimensional structural models of these peptide segments were subsequently generated using the SWISS-MODEL homology modeling server through BLAST and HHblits template selection algorithms. Model reliability was confirmed through rigorous structural validation criteria, requiring favorable MolProbity scores, Ramachandran plot favored percentages of 98 percent or greater, sequence identities exceeding 40 percent, and QMEAN Z-scores higher than negative 4.0. To eliminate structural redundancy, root-mean-square distance calculations were performed in PyMOL software to determine structural convergence among predicted peptide conformations. This structural filtering selected six representative viral sequences: strain A0A0D4D8J0 for segment 45 to 65, strain A0A0N7H514 for segment 110 to 140, strain A0A0D4D8J0 for segments 190 to 225 and 300 to 345, strain A0A0D4D9E3 for segment 255 to 290, and strain J9WMM0 for segment 346 to 390. Active binding crevices within these peptide models were mapped computationally using the CASTp 3.0 server configured with a default radius probe of 1.4 angstroms. Parallel to the viral target preparation, the researchers compiled a curated library of seventy-one plant-derived bioactive antiviral compounds from peer-reviewed literature, retrieving their canonical SMILES notations and three-dimensional spatial structures from the PubChem chemical database. The entire library underwent rigorous virtual ADMET screening via the ADMETlab 2.0 platform to evaluate human intestinal absorption, cellular permeability, metabolic clearance, half-life parameters, blood-brain barrier penetration, and potential organ toxicities. Drug-likeness was evaluated against Lipinski’s rule of five, which specifies a molecular weight below 500 grams per mole, fewer than three hydrogen-bond donors, fewer than twelve hydrogen-bond acceptors, a octanol-water partition coefficient log P below five, and fewer than twelve rotatable bonds. Four candidate molecules successfully satisfied Lipinski rules, the GlaxoSmithKline criteria, and the Golden Triangle rule: the flavone baicalein, the flavonol quercetin, the sesquiterpene lactone artecanin, and the isoflavone genistein. All four demonstrated favorable Caco-2 cell permeability values exceeding negative 5.15, acceptable human hepatotoxicity and skin sensitization profiles, low mutagenic AMES probabilities, and satisfactory drug clearance rates. Rigid molecular docking simulations were executed using the AutoDock 1.5.6 software package across each of the six designated envelope functional pockets, calculating binding free energy values based on classical thermodynamic principles. A uniform grid box measuring 60 by 60 by 60 grid points was constructed in AutoGrid to calculate electrostatic, van der Waals, and solvation energy grids. Across all evaluated active pockets, the four shortlisted phytochemicals displayed pronounced docking affinities, yet genistein consistently registered the strongest overall binding scores. For pocket 45 to 65, baicalein and quercetin both docked with negative 4.6 kilocalories per mole, artecanin with negative 4.4 kilocalories per mole, and genistein with negative 4.9 kilocalories per mole. In the 110 to 140 pocket, baicalein recorded negative 4.7 kilocalories per mole, while quercetin, artecanin, and genistein achieved negative 5.0 kilocalories per mole. In the 190 to 225 pocket, binding values were negative 6.6 kilocalories per mole for baicalein, negative 7.0 for quercetin, negative 6.4 for artecanin, and negative 7.1 for genistein. Docking continued across the remaining three envelope regions, showing consistent intermolecular affinity. In pocket 255 to 290, baicalein scored negative 5.7 kilocalories per mole, artecanin negative 5.6 kilocalories per mole, and both quercetin and genistein negative 5.9 kilocalories per mole. In pocket 300 to 345, baicalein and genistein reached negative 6.0 kilocalories per mole, while quercetin and artecanin reached negative 5.9 kilocalories per mole. Most notably, within the 346 to 390 pocket, genistein established the strongest overall interaction, reaching a binding energy of negative 7.6 kilocalories per mole, outperforming baicalein at negative 7.1 kilocalories per mole, quercetin at negative 7.0 kilocalories per mole, and artecanin at negative 6.8 kilocalories per mole. Across all tested envelope sites, genistein displayed an average binding affinity of negative 6.06 plus or minus 1.1 kilocalories per mole. Within the high-affinity 346 to 390 site of strain J9WMM0, molecular visualization using Discovery Studio revealed an intricate interactome comprising seven van der Waals contacts with threonine 1, leucine 6, proline 26, glutamic acid 30, serine 31, tyrosine 32, and isoleucine 33, alongside a vital hydrogen bond with glutamine 2, and three pi-alkyl linkages involving arginine 5, alanine 24, and proline 27. To investigate whether this top-performing complex could preserve structural stability in a realistic aqueous environment, the researchers conducted 100-nanosecond molecular dynamics simulations using the GROMACS package under the CHARMM27 force field. The genistein-peptide complex was solvated in an explicit TIP3P water cubic box measuring 90.0 by 90.0 by 90.0 nanometers, neutralized with sodium and chloride counter-ions, and energy-minimized to eliminate steric clashes. Simulations ran at a regulated temperature of 300 Kelvin and atmospheric pressure of 1 atmosphere, utilizing the Nose-Hoover thermostat, the Martyna-Tobias-Klein barostat, and particle mesh Ewald electrostatics with a grid spacing of 0.8 angstroms. Trajectory coordinates were logged every 1000 picoseconds, allowing detailed measurement of root-mean-square deviation, root-mean-square fluctuation, radius of gyration, solvent-accessible surface area, and intermolecular hydrogen bonding throughout the 100-nanosecond duration. Analysis of the simulation trajectories corroborated the structural integrity and conformational stability of the genistein-envelope complex. Root-mean-square deviation of the complex equilibrated during the initial 10 nanoseconds and remained stable between 0.7 and 0.8 nanometers from 20 to 60 nanoseconds. Although a minor elevation toward 1.6 nanometers appeared after 80 nanoseconds, the trajectory re-stabilized near 1.1 nanometers toward the simulation endpoint, confirming persistent ligand containment without displacement from the active pocket. Residue-level root-mean-square fluctuation plots revealed that while terminal peptide ends exhibited expected flexibility near 0.8 nanometers, core interacting residues displayed restrained fluctuations between 0.2 and 0.4 nanometers. Furthermore, the radius of gyration maintained a narrow range of 1.03 to 1.27 nanometers, demonstrating sustained structural compactness. Solvent-accessible surface area values fluctuated steadily between 38 and 48 square nanometers, indicating reliable solvent exposure and stable peptide folding. Intermolecular hydrogen bonding remained resilient, typically exhibiting one to three continuous hydrogen bonds and intermittently reaching four to five contacts, while principal component analysis confirmed tightly clustered conformational dynamics. Thermodynamic stability was further quantified through Molecular Mechanics/Generalized Born Surface Area calculations using the GMX_MMPBSA tool, which revealed a favorable net binding free energy of approximately negative 18 kilocalories per mole. Gas-phase molecular mechanics contributions totaled roughly negative 35 kilocalories per mole, dominated by favorable van der Waals interactions of approximately negative 25 kilocalories per mole and electrostatic interactions contributing negative 10 kilocalories per mole, illustrating strong hydrophobic packing. Although the total polar solvation energy presented an unfavorable barrier of approximately positive 20 kilocalories per mole, it was partly compensated by favorable non-polar solvation of negative 3 kilocalories per mole, ensuring an overall spontaneous binding state. While genistein occurs widely in dietary legumes, particularly mature soybeans yielding between 5.6 and 276 milligrams per 100 grams, the study authors emphasize that their computational findings are strictly dry-lab predictions. Wet-lab experimental investigations, including in vitro viral plaque reduction neutralization assays and subsequent in vivo trials, remain essential before any clinical antiviral therapeutic claims can be established. In an investigation conducted using Huh-7 human hepatocellular carcinoma cells, researchers evaluated how blocking the exportin 1, or XPO1, nuclear export pathway affects the trafficking of the viral non-structural protein 3, known as NS3, alongside its downstream consequences on mitochondrial dynamics and innate antiviral defenses. Although orthoflavivirus replication cycles operate predominantly within the host cytoplasm in association with membranes derived from the endoplasmic reticulum, viral factors routinely transit into the cellular nucleus. Rather than restricting viral propagation, targeted pharmacological disruption of XPO1-mediated export drove the accumulation of NS3 in both nuclear and mitochondrial compartments, reorganized mitochondrial architecture into elongated networks, and blunted type I interferon secretion, establishing a distinctly pro-viral environment in vitro. The study specifically addressed how nucleocytoplasmic transport mechanics influence the intracellular sorting of dengue virus non-structural protein 3, a multifunctional enzyme possessing essential viral protease and helicase activities required for polyprotein processing and RNA replication. Previous investigations had established that dengue virus proteins, notably the polymerase NS5 and the protease-helicase NS3, utilize classical importin pathways to access the nucleus during the initial phases of infection, where they degrade structural nucleoporins within the nuclear pore complex and interfere with host transcriptional networks. While earlier strategies aimed at blocking nuclear import with compounds such as ivermectin succeeded in restricting viral replication, the precise role played by nuclear export pathways and their structural link to extra-nuclear organelles had remained largely uncharacterized. The research team explored whether obstructing nuclear export would cause dengue virus NS3 to redistribute abnormally between the cell nucleus and the mitochondrial network, and whether this trafficking bottleneck altered organellar integrity and cellular immune competence. To evaluate these transport mechanisms, the scientists propagated dengue virus type 2, using the New Guinea C reference strain, alongside a comparative Zika virus strain, using neonatal CD-1 suckling mouse brains under approved institutional animal care protocols. These neonatal murine brain tissues served strictly as an in vivo viral propagation substrate rather than an animal disease model, yielding clarified viral stocks for downstream cell culture experiments. Cultured human Huh-7 cells, maintained in high-glucose Advanced Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium supplemented with fetal bovine serum and antibiotics, were infected with dengue virus type 2 or Zika virus at a multiplicity of infection of five. Alongside authentic infections, the authors also introduced plasmid constructs encoding dengue virus NS2B-NS3 into uninfected Huh-7 cells through electroporation, permitting the examination of NS3 sorting and mitochondrial alterations independent of the full viral replication cycle or secondary structural proteins. Using transmission immunoelectron microscopy with colloidal gold-labeled antibodies, the investigators systematically mapped the subcellular locations of NS3 in Huh-7 cells at twelve and twenty-four hours post-infection. In cells infected with dengue virus type 2, colloidal gold particles indicating NS3 were clearly resolved not only throughout the cytoplasm and the nucleus but also directly within the interior of mitochondria. Quantitative assessment revealed that 17.5 percent of mitochondria were positive for NS3 gold labeling at twelve hours post-infection, an abundance that expanded to 27.5 percent of mitochondria by twenty-four hours. In sharp contrast, parallel experiments performed in Zika virus-infected Huh-7 cells showed that zero percent of mitochondria contained NS3 gold particles at either time point, even though Zika virus NS3 readily accumulated within the cytoplasm and nucleus. Multiple sequence alignment of orthoflavivirus proteins demonstrated that a defined mitochondrial targeting sequence, previously reported in dengue virus serotype 1 NS3, is preserved across dengue serotypes but lacks sufficient sequence conservation in Zika virus NS3, explaining the striking disparity in organellar tropism between the two viruses. To probe the dependence of NS3 distribution on cellular export mechanisms, the researchers employed two distinct small-molecule inhibitors of XPO1: leptomycin B, an irreversible covalent inhibitor binding cysteine 528 of the transport receptor, and selinexor, a reversible first-generation selective inhibitor of nuclear export developed for clinical oncology. Treatment of Huh-7 cells with 37 nanomolar leptomycin B for twenty-four hours was first validated using indirect immunofluorescence confocal microscopy and subcellular fractionation assays targeting cyclin B1, an endogenous cellular cargo that relies strictly on XPO1 for nuclear clearance. Whereas cyclin B1 remained predominantly cytoplasmic in vehicle-treated controls, leptomycin B caused marked nuclear retention. Western blot analysis of isolated nuclear and cytoplasmic fractions demonstrated that XPO1 inhibition produced a substantial increase of dengue virus NS3 inside the nucleus. Intriguingly, western blots of purified mitochondrial fractions, validated for purity using the mitochondrial marker TOMM22 alongside nuclear and cytoplasmic controls, demonstrated that leptomycin B treatment concurrently elevated NS3 levels within mitochondria, a finding corroborated in electroporated cells expressing recombinant NS2B3. The scientists next determined how pharmacological export blockade altered mitochondrial ultrastructure. Transmission electron microscopy revealed that uninfected, vehicle-treated Huh-7 cells possessed predominantly small, rounded, or short mitochondria. Following twenty-four hours of exposure to either 37 nanomolar leptomycin B or 200 nanomolar selinexor, uninfected cells exhibited pronounced mitochondrial elongation, reflected by statistically significant increases in total mitochondrial cross-sectional area. Two-dimensional morphometric analysis of confocal images stained for TOMM22 confirmed this remodeling, showing substantial rises in mitochondrial surface area, perimeter length, and network branching index following XPO1 inhibition. When Huh-7 cells were infected with dengue virus type 2 in the absence of inhibitors, mitochondria likewise underwent marked elongation compared to uninfected controls, matching previous observations of virus-induced organelle reshaping. While treating infected cells with leptomycin B or selinexor induced thinner mitochondrial profiles and some structural cristae disorganization, the inhibitors did not amplify the overall elongation beyond the pronounced morphological transformation already driven by dengue infection itself. Because mitochondrial remodeling frequently coincides with changes in organelle turnover and mitochondrial biogenesis, the authors examined mitochondrial mass and biogenesis signaling pathways following XPO1 inhibition. Flow cytometry measurements of Huh-7 cells stained for the outer mitochondrial membrane marker TOMM22 showed that while roughly 60 to 70 percent of cells remained positive across all groups, mean fluorescence intensity rose significantly in uninfected cells treated with leptomycin B or selinexor, indicating an increase in overall mitochondrial mass at the population level. Flow cytometry also revealed that the frequency of dengue-infected cells, identified by intracellular NS3 positivity at twenty-four hours post-infection, expanded from 15 percent in vehicle-treated controls to 26 percent following leptomycin B exposure. Total cellular levels of NS3 protein rose in parallel on western blots. When investigating peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha, or PGC1-alpha, the master transcriptional regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis, researchers detected a modest, non-significant trend toward elevated protein abundance in treated cells and a transient increase in PGC1-alpha messenger RNA in mock-infected cultures, suggesting that biogenesis pathways may be modestly engaged but remain preliminary under these experimental settings. The downstream consequences of nuclear export blockade directly favored viral proliferation rather than antiviral defense. Transmission electron microscopy of dengue virus-infected Huh-7 cells treated with leptomycin B or selinexor revealed a pronounced proliferation of virus-induced cytoplasmic replication vesicles compared to untreated infected cells. Plaque-forming unit assays conducted on cell culture supernatants showed that both leptomycin B and selinexor significantly increased the output of infectious dengue virus type 2 virions. Quantitative reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction assays measuring intracellular viral genomes demonstrated an approximate two-fold increase in viral RNA copies following leptomycin B exposure and a six-fold increase in cells treated with selinexor. Notably, this pro-viral enhancement was entirely specific to dengue virus; parallel viral yield assays and focus-forming unit titrations carried out in Zika virus-infected Huh-7 cells showed no significant alterations in infectious particle release or viral RNA accumulation after XPO1 inhibition. To resolve how blocking nuclear export accelerated dengue replication despite triggering cellular stress, the investigators examined the modulation of the type I interferon signaling cascade. Unstimulated Huh-7 cells exhibited minimal baseline interferon activation, prompting the team to pre-stimulate cells with twenty micrograms per milliliter of recombinant human interferon-beta for six hours before virus inoculation. Pre-stimulated cells were subsequently infected with dengue virus type 2 and treated with vehicle, leptomycin B, or selinexor for twenty-four hours. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays performed on cell culture supernatants revealed that pre-stimulated, infected cells treated with either nuclear export inhibitor suffered an approximate 50 percent decrease in secreted interferon-beta protein compared to untreated stimulated controls. Paradoxically, quantitative reverse-transcription PCR demonstrated a two- to four-fold elevation in interferon-beta and interferon-stimulated gene IFI44L transcripts across treated cells, indicating that while transcription was initiated, post-transcriptional stages such as mRNA nuclear export, protein translation, or cytokine secretion were severely disrupted by XPO1 inhibition. This sharp reduction in functional interferon-beta secretion directly uncoupled the host cell’s antiviral defense from viral control. In untreated Huh-7 cells, interferon-beta pre-stimulation successfully suppressed dengue virus type 2 particle release into the culture medium. However, when cells were treated with leptomycin B or selinexor, infectious viral titers increased significantly even in the presence of prior interferon priming, overcoming the established antiviral state. The authors contextualize these results by noting that while selinexor promotes proteasomal degradation of XPO1 and leptomycin B covalently modifies the receptor without reducing total XPO1 abundance, both agents elicited matching increases in viral titer, NS3 organellar redistribution, and suppression of cytokine output. The researchers caution that these findings are derived from in vitro human hepatoma cell cultures and neonatal mouse brain propagation stocks, meaning clinical extrapolations regarding selective nuclear export inhibitors in human dengue pathology must account for complex tissue-specific immune responses and differences in viral replication kinetics across distinct host systems. content: Florida Dengue Cases Reach 651, Experts Warn About Mosquitoes Breeding in Backyards Florida homeowners may have more to worry about than weeds and pests hiding in their gardens. A growing dengue outbreak has brought new attention to the small pools of standing water where disease-carrying mosquitoes can breed, including places people might overlook during routine yard maintenance. According to the latest Florida Department of Health surveillance figures, the state has recorded 651 locally acquired dengue cases across 12 counties in 2026. The outbreak is the largest reported in the continental United States in decades, with infections far exceeding Florida's previous annual record of 199 cases in 2023. The outbreak has been concentrated around Tampa Bay, with Hillsborough County accounting for 487 cases and neighboring Pinellas County reporting 116 as of November 14. Although the latest weekly figures suggest infections may be slowing, Hillsborough County has extended its local state of emergency through November 26. Health experts also warn that official case counts may underestimate the true number of infections. For residents, the concern extends beyond neighborhoods with confirmed cases. The mosquito species responsible for much of dengue transmission can reproduce around ordinary homes, turning flowerpot saucers, clogged gutters, and forgotten outdoor containers into potential breeding sites. Hidden Around Homes Embedded media follows; please allow a moment to load. Unlike mosquitoes associated with large ponds or marshes, Aedes aegypti, a major mosquito species responsible for dengue transmission, is well adapted to living near people. It lays eggs along the inside walls of containers that collect water, making residential properties suitable places for reproduction. Kevin Sukovich, a licensed pest control operator who owns Clermont-based Webenex, told the Clermont Sun that homeowners play an important role in controlling these mosquitoes, even when county crews are spraying public areas. "The county can spray the streets, but this mosquito breeds in a bottle cap of water behind your grill," Sukovich said. "Nobody owns that part. The homeowner does." The CDC recommends inspecting outdoor spaces at least once a week. Birdbaths, buckets, children's toys, discarded tires, and flowerpot saucers should be emptied and scrubbed to remove mosquito eggs. Simply pouring out the water may leave eggs attached to the container. Gardeners should pay particular attention to areas where water collects unnoticed. Rain barrels need tight-fitting covers or fine mesh screens, while gutters should be kept clear so water can drain. Water-holding plants and containers also deserve attention, especially in shaded sections of the yard. Beyond Backyard Spraying Removing breeding sites is an important first step, but it does not eliminate every mosquito already living around a property. According to CDC mosquito-control guidance, adult mosquitoes can shelter in dark, humid locations, including beneath patio furniture and around garages. Targeted insecticide treatments may help control them, although products must be used according to their labels. For water that cannot be drained or covered, the agency recommends appropriately labeled mosquito larvicides. These target immature mosquitoes before they become flying adults. Homeowners should select products intended for the particular location rather than applying pesticides indiscriminately around ornamental plants, wildlife habitats, or water features. Personal protection matters, too. Aedes mosquitoes can bite during daylight hours, meaning gardeners are not necessarily safe just because they avoid going outside at dusk. EPA-registered insect repellents, long sleeves, and well-maintained window screens can reduce exposure while residents work outdoors or relax on patios. When Bites Become Serious Dengue can cause fever, severe headaches, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, nausea, and rashes. However, not everyone who becomes infected develops noticeable symptoms. Health experts caution that reported cases may underestimate the outbreak's true extent because some infections cause mild symptoms or no symptoms at all. Reporting delays can also make it difficult to measure the outbreak while cases are being investigated. According to WUSF's November 20 report, Florida recorded 27 additional locally acquired cases during the latest reporting week, down from 100 in the preceding report. Although most people with symptomatic dengue recover, the infection can occasionally progress to severe illness involving bleeding, fluid leakage, or shock. The CDC advises seeking emergency medical care for warning signs such as persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, or unusual bleeding, particularly after a fever begins to subside. There is no specific antiviral treatment for dengue. The CDC recommends rest, adequate fluids, and acetaminophen to help manage fever and pain. People who have or may have dengue should avoid aspirin and ibuprofen because these medications can increase the risk of bleeding. Anyone who suspects they have dengue should contact a healthcare professional for evaluation and guidance. Preventing the Problem For Florida homeowners, preventing mosquito bites begins with paying attention to the places where mosquitoes reproduce. A forgotten bucket, clogged gutter, or water-filled flowerpot saucer can provide breeding conditions even in an otherwise well-maintained yard. With hundreds of locally acquired dengue infections already reported this year, a weekly inspection of outdoor spaces is a simple precaution worth taking. Removing standing water, maintaining screens, and using appropriate insect repellent can help reduce exposure while residents continue enjoying their gardens. Want more articles like this one? Bridges USA TODAY Updated Nov. 23, 2026, 9:50 a.m. ET More than 600 cases of locally acquired dengue have been reported this year in Florida, according to the Florida Department of Health's Weekly Arbovirus Surveillance Report. The report for the period from Nov. 8 through Nov. 14 says that "651 cases of locally acquired dengue and 22 mosquito pools have been reported from 12 counties" in 2026. More than 600 cases of locally acquired dengue have been reported this year in Florida, according to the Florida Department of Health's Weekly Arbovirus Surveillance Report. The report for the period from Nov. 8 through Nov. 14 says that "651 cases of locally acquired dengue and 22 mosquito pools have been reported from 12 counties" in 2026. From Nov. 8 through Nov. 14 alone, 27 cases of locally acquired dengue were reported in Florida. Hillsborough County saw 487 of the 651 reported locally acquired dengue cases this year. Brevard County saw one case, Broward County saw one case, Citrus County saw three cases, Manatee County saw two cases, Miami-Dade saw 16 cases, Orange County saw 15 cases, Palm Beach County saw one case, Pasco County saw six cases, Pinellas County saw 116 cases, Polk County saw one case and Seminole County saw two cases. Florida's outbreak far exceeds the previous largest outbreak, which was 264 local cases in Hawaii's Big Island between September 2015 and March 2016. Dengue is also known as dengue fever or breakbone fever, the latter due to the pain it can cause. It can present as "a flu-like illness with severe muscle aches and joint pain," along with fever and "sometimes" a rash, according to the Florida Department of Health in Miami-Dade County. Symptoms of dengue will appear within 14 days of being bitten by an infected mosquito. Dengue is not contagious, and is transmitted via the bite of an infected Aedes aegypti mosquito. Dengue cases continue to climb in Florida According to Florida Department of Health data released Nov. 14, 12 counties have reported 651 locally acquired dengue cases, up from 624 reported Nov. 13. One new case of west Nile virus was reported over the past week in Holmes County. Dengue: 651 cases 487 in Hillsborough County 116 in Pinellas County 16 in Miami-Dade County 15 in Orange County 6 in Pasco County 3 in Citrus County 2 in Manatee County 2 in Seminole County 1 in Brevard County 1 in Broward County 1 in Palm Beach County 1 in Polk County West Nile: 10 cases 2 in Alachua County 2 in Duval County (including one asymptomatic blood donor) 1 in Columbia County 2 in Holmes County 1 in Leon (asymptomatic blood donor) 1 in Sarasota County 1 in Walton County Chikungunya: 2 cases 2 in Miami-Dade County Eastern Equine Encephalitis: 1 case 1 in Leon County How to best prevent mosquito-borne illnesses In June, Miami-Dade County encouraged residents to "take proactive steps" to prevent the spread of mosquito-borne illnesses, including "frequently checking for and eliminating any standing water." That's the best protection against "container-breeding mosquitoes," said a press release by the county, which are the "likeliest species to transmit the viruses that cause dengue, chikungunya, Zika, and yellow fever," illnesses that are among those most commonly transmitted by mosquitoes. Standing water usually accumulates after rainfall or irrigation in items like potted planters, saucers, outdoor toys, coolers and boat/car tarps, according to the release. "As little as one teaspoon or bottle cap of water standing for more than one week is enough for mosquitoes to breed and multiply," according to a flyer provided by the FDOH. As for individual protection, mosquito repellent can help prevent bites while outdoors, especially between "dusk and dawn," when mosquitoes are most active. The county also suggests: Covering entrances to one's home, including windows and doors, with mesh screens. Wearing clothes with long sleeves and pant legs to "maximize skin protection." Regularly cleaning rain gutters to avoid water pooling within them. Filling up indentations in one's lawn, air conditioner drain areas and tree holes. Regularly replacing water in outdoor pet dishes and birdbaths. Requesting a mosquito inspection via the county’s online portal. MCCD data for 2025 is yet to be released.The gap is also evident nationally. The MCCD report recorded 2,340 medically certified dengue deaths in 2024, compared with just 297 in the Union Health Ministry’s NCVBDC surveillance system. OffOn Stream on Scientists report strong new evidence that specially bred mosquitoes can fend off dengue There is new evidence that breeding a special kind of mosquito could help fend off dengue infections, rather than solely relying on pesticides and trying to avoid getting bitten ByLAURAN NEERGAARD AP medical writer November 21, 2026, 12:35 AM WASHINGTON -- Children who lived in Brazilian neighborhoods buzzing with a special kind of mosquito were far less likely to catch dengue or another worrisome virus, chikungunya, researchers reported Saturday. The major study of more than 5,700 children in one of the world’s dengue hot spots offers new evidence that breeding mosquitoes unable to transmit these viruses can be a viable strategy rather than solely relying on pesticides and trying to avoid getting bitten. In neighborhoods populated by these so-called Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes, researchers found about a 69% reduction in dengue and chikungunya infections in schoolchildren compared to similar neighborhoods — an effect sustained even during Brazil’s severe 2024 dengue outbreak, said Dr. Sri Edupuganti of Emory University, part of the international research team. The researchers reported the findings at a meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene. “This is really exciting,” said Dr. David Hamer, a global health expert at Boston University who wasn’t involved with the Brazilian study. He predicts that pairing more use of these Wolbachia mosquitoes with existing steps to fight mosquito-borne disease could “knock dengue down to much lower levels” in many places. The latest research comes as Florida grapples with an unusually large outbreak of the virus, what appears to be the biggest in any U.S. state since at least the 1940s. Usually in the continental U.S., dengue is found mostly in people who traveled internationally. But as of Friday, Florida health officials had tallied more than 650 locally acquired cases, about three-quarters of them in Hillsborough County, home to Tampa. Outside the U.S., the nonprofit World Mosquito Program has pioneered the Wolbachia strategy. How it works: Scientists breed mosquitoes to carry a kind of bacteria called Wolbachia. It is harmless to people and common in many insects, although not dengue-carrying Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. The bacteria dramatically reduce the mosquitoes’ ability to transmit certain viruses. Female mosquitoes spread the bacteria to their offspring, so releasing enough of the specially bred insects — males and females — into an area allows Wolbachia to gradually become established in the local mosquito population. But because people with mild symptoms may not be diagnosed, the new study in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, went further. Researchers tested blood for signs of dengue, chikungunya or the Zika virus. The four-year study compared children living in neighborhoods that all got the same pesticide and other mosquito-control interventions, but half were randomly assigned to have Wolbachia mosquitoes released into the area. Log in A specially bred mosquito appears to offer strong protection against dengue and chikungunya, according to a new study, as cases of mosquito-borne illnesses spike in Florida. The major study of more than 5,700 children in Brazil, one of the world's dengue hot spots, offers new evidence that breeding mosquitoes unable to transmit viruses can be a viable new strategy instead of relying on pesticides and trying to avoid getting bitten. Dr Sri Edupuganti of Emory University, part of the international research team, said children in neighborhoods populated by Wolbachia-carrying insects showed about a 69% reduction in dengue and chikungunya infections compared with similar neighborhoods. open image in gallery Scientists bred mosquitoes to carry a kind of bacteria called Wolbachia (Getty Images/iStockphoto) The effect was sustained even during Brazil's severe 2024 dengue outbreak, she said. The findings were reported at a meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene. Florida grapples with large outbreak The latest research comes as Florida grapples with an unusually large outbreak of the virus, what appears to be the biggest in any U.S. state since at least the 1940s. Outside the U.S., the nonprofit World Mosquito Program has pioneered the Wolbachia strategy. Scientists breed mosquitoes to carry a kind of bacteria called Wolbachia. How Wolbachia strategy works The bacteria are harmless to people and common in many insects, although not dengue-carrying Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. Wolbachia dramatically reduce the mosquitoes' ability to transmit certain viruses. Female mosquitoes spread the bacteria to their offspring, so releasing enough of the specially bred insects, males and females, into an area allows Wolbachia to gradually become established in the local mosquito population. Field trials and other studies in Indonesia and elsewhere have shown the strategy can significantly lower dengue diagnoses. The evaluation focused on synthesizing available evidence to determine how accurately the index reflects severe or complicated conditions based on definitions applied within existing clinical literature. To investigate the performance of the test, investigators conducted a systematic search across seven electronic databases from their inception through March 13, 2026. Eligible studies were required to evaluate the index specifically among patients with laboratory-confirmed dengue infections. The review adhered strictly to the methodological standards outlined in the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses of Diagnostic Test Accuracy Studies guidance. The study selection process identified eight eligible investigations for qualitative synthesis, from which six studies encompassing a total of 948 participants provided sufficient data to be pooled quantitatively. Study-level sensitivity and specificity values were calculated directly from extracted or reconstructed two-by-two contingency tables. Pooled summary estimates were then derived using a frequentist bivariate random-effects Reitsma model fitted via restricted maximum likelihood estimation. Across the pooled primary analysis of six studies, the index yielded a summary sensitivity of 0.75, with a 95 percent confidence interval spanning from 0.66 to 0.82. The corresponding summary specificity was 0.80, with a 95 percent confidence interval ranging from 0.76 to 0.84. In addition, the pooled positive likelihood ratio was estimated at 3.76, while the negative likelihood ratio was 0.32, producing an overall diagnostic odds ratio of 12.42. Evaluation of global discriminative capacity established an area under the summary receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.841. Stability of these statistical results was assessed through leave-one-out sensitivity analyses, which generated comparable performance estimates across iterations. In a separate sensitivity analysis restricted to four studies specifically comparing severe dengue against non-severe dengue, the model calculated a sensitivity of 0.73, a specificity of 0.79, and an area under the curve of 0.821. The researchers cautioned that these pooled accuracy figures reflect a heterogeneous target condition and must not be interpreted as applying exclusively to strictly defined severe dengue classifications. Substantial variation in clinical target definitions alongside a broad range of retrospectively selected index thresholds currently constrain direct clinical applicability. Because retrospective cutoff selection can overestimate diagnostic accuracy, rigorous prospective validation remains essential before the index can be routinely implemented alongside standard clinical assessments and serial laboratory monitoring. In their detailed evaluation of diagnostic performance, the investigators systematically assessed potential heterogeneity and threshold effects across the gathered investigations. content: Florida reported one new human case of West Nile virus infection in Holmes County during the week of Nov. 8-14, while locally acquired dengue cases and mosquito-borne illness advisories remained widespread across the state. State arbovirus surveillance also recorded 27 locally acquired dengue cases and 29 travel-associated dengue cases this week. No human cases of St. Louis encephalitis or eastern equine encephalitis were reported this week. Sixteen sentinel chickens tested positive for antibodies to West Nile virus in Alachua, Bay, Brevard, Citrus, Hernando, Indian River, Leon, Pasco, Pinellas, Sarasota, Sumter and Walton counties. Two sentinel chickens tested positive for antibodies to eastern equine encephalitis in Bay and Leon counties. Florida had 651 locally acquired dengue cases in 2026, with cases reported in Brevard, Broward, Citrus, Hillsborough, Manatee, Miami-Dade, Orange, Palm Beach, Pasco, Pinellas, Polk and Seminole counties. Travel-associated chikungunya fever cases reached 114, while two locally acquired chikungunya fever cases were reported in Miami-Dade County with onset in August. No locally acquired Zika fever cases were reported this week or in 2026. No travel-associated Oropouche fever or Zika fever cases were reported this week. As of Nov. 14, Bay, Brevard, Broward, Columbia, Leon, Manatee, Martin, Palm Beach, Polk, Sarasota and Walton counties were under a mosquito-borne illness advisory. Alachua, Citrus, Duval, Hillsborough, Holmes, Miami-Dade, Orange, Pasco, Pinellas and Seminole counties were under a mosquito-borne illness alert. No veterinary cases were reported this week. content: India Cities Delhi Mumbai Kolkata +5 more World US UK Europe Asia +3 more Entertainment Bollywood South OTT TV +3 more Sports Cricket Hockey Football Pickleball +7 more Business Personal Finance Markets Companies Economy Lifestyle Relationships Health Fashion Books +3 more Videos India World Shows Newshour +5 more More Latest News Education Auto Opinion Viral Viral 26 Nov 2026 | 08:28 AM IST Live TV SIGN IN Latest India World Entertainment Sports Business Lifestyle Opinion Pickleball Tech Videos Viral US-Iran War Live UpdatesUP Election Seat-Sharing HeatStock Market TodayRamayana Box Office CollectionToyota Innova Hycross Facelift Launch TodayDelhi AQI Today Search "Sporting Vs Man Utd" Health Can Mosquitoes Help Fight Dengue Instead Of Spreading It? Authored by: Simran Sukhnani Updated: Nov 25, 2026, 13:01 IST Scientists are using Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes to fight dengue, with Brazil reporting promising results. Here's how this unusual approach works and whether it could help India tackle outbreaks. Can mosquitos help prevent dengue (Credits: iStock) follow usfollow us Scientists have reported a promising breakthrough in the fight against mosquito-borne diseases, and it involves using mosquitoes themselves as a weapon. In Brazil, specially bred mosquitoes carrying a naturally occurring bacterium called Wolbachia were associated with a 69% reduction in dengue and chikungunya infections among children exposed to them. The findings have sparked fresh interest in an approach that could change how the world tackles mosquito-borne diseases. The idea sounds unusual - instead of killing mosquitoes, scientists are releasing mosquitoes that are less capable of spreading infections. But how does this work, and could it make a difference in countries like India, where dengue outbreaks remain a recurring public health concern? How Do Wolbachia-Infected Mosquitoes Work? Wolbachia is a naturally occurring bacterium found in several insect species. It is introduced into Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, the primary carriers of dengue, chikungunya and Zika viruses. Once established inside the mosquito, the bacterium makes it harder for these viruses to multiply and reach the mosquito's saliva, reducing the likelihood of transmission when it bites a human. The important difference here is that these mosquitoes are not genetically modified to become a different species, nor are they designed to eliminate mosquitoes altogether. The objective is to make the existing mosquito population less capable of transmitting disease. The bacterium also has an interesting way of sustaining itself. Female mosquitoes pass Wolbachia on to their offspring, allowing it to gradually establish itself in local mosquito populations. This means the intervention does not necessarily require repeated releases indefinitely once the bacterium becomes established. What Did The Brazil Study Find? The latest findings come from a four-year study conducted in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, involving more than 5,700 children. Researchers compared neighbourhoods where Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes had been released with similar neighbourhoods that continued to receive conventional mosquito-control interventions. What is the Wolbachia bacterium in mosquitos (Credits: iStock) The study found approximately 69% fewer dengue and chikungunya infections among children in areas where Wolbachia mosquitoes were released. The reduction reportedly persisted even during Brazil's severe dengue outbreak in 2024. Researchers also tested blood samples to identify infections that might otherwise have gone undetected because of mild or unreported symptoms. The findings were presented at a meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene. Could This Approach Work In India? For a country like India, where dengue outbreaks regularly put pressure on healthcare facilities, the possibility of reducing transmission without relying entirely on insecticides is significant. However, experts believe the approach needs to be understood as an additional layer of protection rather than a replacement for existing preventive measures. Dr. Paritosh Baghel, Senior Consultant Physician at S.L. Raheja Hospital, Mumbai, explains the distinction, "As opposed to traditional methods of mosquito control, which emphasise the eradication of the mosquito populations, this method seeks to inhibit the mosquito populations' ability to spread infections." Dr. Umang Agarwal, Consultant, Infectious Diseases at P.D. Hinduja Hospital and MRC, Khar, believes the approach represents an important shift in disease prevention. "The novelty of the approach is in the fact that, contrary to the elimination of mosquitoes, scientists are now looking for ways to reduce their capabilities to spread diseases," he says. However, there are important considerations before such a strategy can be adopted widely. Its effectiveness depends on successfully establishing Wolbachia in local mosquito populations, and results may vary with geography, mosquito populations and climatic conditions. Dr. Baghel also cautions that promising international findings should not be mistaken for a ready-made solution. India would need appropriate evaluation across its own environmental and epidemiological conditions. Meanwhile, the basics of dengue prevention remain unchanged. Removing stagnant water, preventing mosquito breeding, using repellents and wearing protective clothing are still essential. Recognising symptoms such as persistent fever, severe body pain, vomiting and abdominal pain, and seeking timely medical attention can also help prevent complications. The idea of fighting mosquitoes with mosquitoes may sound counterintuitive, but it offers an interesting possibility: perhaps the answer to controlling some mosquito-borne diseases is not eliminating every mosquito, but changing what they are capable of transmitting. Nov 23, 2026 8 min read By Meg Dalton Afeez Sodeinde with mosquitoes in the Vogels Lab. Photo by Kristen Ortega Listen to this story ‘Wolbachia’ mosquito: The bug that could change everything 0:00 / 9:52 In 2015, Albert Ko spent several months in the maternity hospitals of Salvador, a city in Northeast Brazil where he has been working with the Brazilian Ministry of Health since the 1990s. At that time, the city was the epicenter of a Zika epidemic, which eventually spread throughout the Americas and infected roughly 1.5 million people. Ko witnessed firsthand the impact of this mosquito-borne disease on the local population, which caused severe birth defects in infants whose mothers came from the poorest communities in the city and were infected during pregnancy with the Zika virus. “Our team’s work in Brazil centers on this intersection between infectious disease and social justice,” said Ko, the Albert Ko, the Raj and Indra Nooyi Professor of Public Health at the Yale School of Public Health (YSPH). “In Brazil and many countries, social inequity, combined with rapid urbanization, has led to the emergence of diseases, such as Zika, which disproportionally affect marginalized populations living in urban informal settlements.” The Zika epidemic prompted Ko and his team in Brazil and Yale to tackle the question how to prevent diseases transmitted by the Aedes aegypti mosquito, including dengue and chikungunya as well as Zika, in these vulnerable communities and beyond. Today, Ko, alongside Chantal Vogels, an assistant professor of epidemiology (microbial diseases) at YSPH, are investigating just that. One in the field and the other in the lab, their research uses Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes as a tool for controlling dengue, Zika, and other mosquito-borne diseases. Wolbachia is a naturally occurring bacterium that resides inside some insects. If you introduce Wolbachia into the Aedes aegypti mosquito, which does not naturally harbor the bacteria, it acts as a vaccine and prevents the transmission of viruses, such the dengue virus, within the mosquito. Wolbachia-infected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes being reared at the EVITA trial site in Belo Horizonte Brazil. Photo by Flávio Carvalho As the global climate continues to warm, the work of Ko and Vogels will prove even more critical. More and more communities are seeing upticks in mosquito-borne diseases beyond the tropics, including in the United States. This year, for example, the state of Florida has seen a record number of dengue fever cases, more than 400 so far. In the lab With a background in entomology and virology, Vogels has dedicated her career to studying mosquito and tick-borne viruses. Specifically, she’s focused on understanding the factors that affect transmission and control. “The ultimate goal of my work is to better mitigate the burden of mosquito and tick-borne viruses on public health,” Vogels said. Vogels got interested in studying Wolbachia specifically because it seemed like such a novel method for biological control. She was intrigued by the interplay between viruses like dengue, the Wolbachia bacterium, and mosquitoes. So, she started studying the genetic diversity of viruses and how that variation affects the effectiveness of mosquito control strategies. “I don’t think there’s ever going be a single control intervention,” Vogels said. “You need an integrated approach, and I do think that Wolbachia fits within that toolbox.” Members of Vogels Lab. From left: Chantal Vogels, Julian W. Bakker, Afeez Sodeinde, and Nicole Feriancek. Photo by Kristen Ortega Right now, there are two main strategies that are being used in the field. The first method uses Wolbachia as a form of birth control for the mosquito population. This method relies on mass rearing of large numbers of mosquitoes in the laboratory with Wolbachia which are then released to the wild. Male mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia are not able to produce offspring with the wildtype females. This method suppresses the local mosquito population. “That method relies on continued release of the male mosquitoes,” Vogels said. “When you stop, mosquito populations can reestablish themselves again.” The second method uses Wolbachia as a form of vaccination for mosquitoes. With this method, female Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes are released into the wild. They can have offspring with either Wolbachia-carrying or wildtype males, and because Wolbachia is maternally transmitted, the offspring would also carry Wolbachia in either case. This method replaces the local mosquito population. Initially in the lab, these two methods — suppression and replacement — have been introduced through field trials. In some cases, the results have been good. In other cases, the results have been mixed. That’s where Vogels’s research comes in. In her lab, Vogels and her research team use experimental approaches to understand how Wolbachia can be used to control dengue. They’re able to manipulate different conditions to understand the factors that impact the inhibition that Wolbachia is causing in terms of dengue transmission. “If we know what factors impact control methods like Wolbachia, then we can immediately inform those control interventions and make a big impact in the field,” Vogels said. One of the important factors is the feeding behavior of mosquitoes, or how frequently they have “blood meals,” which refers to the ingestion of blood by female mosquitoes after puncturing the skin of vertebrates. Vogels’s team has found that natural feeding behavior has a reduced effect on Wolbachia in terms of inhibiting dengue. In another study, they looked at how genetic differences in dengue virus impact Wolbachia’s ability to inhibit it. They tested two Wolbachia strains against 60 different dengue virus samples from all four serotypes. They found that both the Wolbachia strains and dengue virus samples varied in how well they worked together, with some pairs inhibiting more effectively than others. Fieldwork As Vogels has been experimenting with these methods in the lab, Ko has been testing them out in the field. He started working in Brazil on Wolbachia interventions in 2017, informed by his experience in mounting the public health response to the Zika epidemic in preceding years. At that time, his friend and fellow researcher, Mauro Teixeira, a professor at the Federal University of Minas Gerais in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, was designing a cluster randomized controlled trial for population replacement, where Wolbachia is used as a form of vaccination for mosquitoes. The duo also worked closely with Luciano Moreira, a senior researcher at the Oswaldo Cruz Foundation, the research branch of the Brazilian Ministry of Health which Ko has been affiliated with for the last 30 years. The EVITA trial team, which includes Mauro Teixeira (eighth from left) from the Federal University of Minas Gerais, Sri Edupuganti (ninth front from left) from Emory University, Derek Cummings (tenth back from left) from Johns Hopkins University, and Albert Ko (third from right), and YSPH doctoral student Elisabeth Nelson (fourth back from left). Paloma Carcamo, another YSPH doctoral student, was not present. Credit: Luciano Moreira and Flávio Carvalho The trial, called EVITA, launched in 2020 with funding support from the National Institutes of Health and Brazilian Ministry of Health. Their approach involved replacing the native mosquito population with Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes, which are resistant to dengue, chikungunya and Zika viruses. With this approach, researchers only have to release the mosquitoes once, rather than continuously releasing infected male mosquitoes to suppress mosquito populations, which can be costly and challenging to do in resource-poor settings, particularly in the Global South. For the trial, the EVITA team designated 58 clusters, or neighborhoods surrounding primary schools within the city of Belo Horizonte, which is home to 3 million people. Moreira and his team grew colonies of Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes, and by car and motorcycle, released them in half of the neighborhoods. In total, 32 million mosquitoes were released during the trial. Teixeira and his team then followed the school children living in both the neighborhoods that received the intervention and those that did not to evaluate whether they had a dengue or chikungunya infection. EVITA team implementing patient enrollment and protocol in neighborhoods at the trial’s start during the pandemic in 2020. Credit: Luciano Moreira and Flávio Carvalho “The primary outcome was to determine the effectiveness of preventing infection with dengue or chikungunya in schoolchildren living in neighborhoods where Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes were released,” said Ko, who is also a professor of medicine (infectious diseases) at Yale School of Medicine. After the conclusion of the EVITA trial, in 2024, an international team of investigators — including Teixeira, Moreira, Ko, and YSPH doctoral students, Elisabeth Nelson and Paloma Carcamo — spent the past two years analyzing the findings. The findings — which were presented at the meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene on Nov. 21, 2026 — showed that the intervention worked; it reduced the risk of infection with dengue by 69% and infection with chikungunya by 73%. Perhaps more impressive, researchers say, the Wolbachia population replacement prevented infections during the largest epidemic of dengue in recorded history in Brazil, which occurred in the trial’s last year in 2024. “The 2024 epidemic was a pressure test that demonstrated that Wolbachia population replacement protected communities even under conditions of intense transmission,” Ko said. They also demonstrated that the intervention not only prevented dengue and chikungunya infections among school children but also significantly reduced the number cases of dengue and chikungunya in all age groups who sought medical care at health posts or were hospitalized. “The EVITA trial is an important step forward in the search for sustainable, scalable approaches to protecting people from dengue, chikungunya and Zika,” Ko said. “Over 4 billion of the world’s population live in regions, including parts of the U.S., where diseases transmitted by the Aedes aegypti mosquito occur and this number will increase because of future trends in climate change and urbanization.” Health & Medicine Solutions How to prepare youth to respond to firearm injury risk Nov 25, 2026 4 min read Discoveries Can a common blood thinner stop osteoarthritis? content: News Around the World Brazil study links Wolbachia bacterium to 69% reduction in infections — The Independent UA.NEWS 21 November 2026 17:31 A study in the Brazilian city of Belo Horizonte involving more than 5,700 children found an approximately 69% lower incidence of dengue and chikungunya infections in areas with mosquitoes carrying the Wolbachia bacterium than in similar areas. As The Independent reports , this effect persisted even during a severe dengue outbreak in Brazil in 2024. The results were reported by Dr. Shri Edupuganti of Emory University, who was part of the international research team. The findings were presented at a meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene. How Wolbachia works Scientists breed mosquitoes that carry Wolbachia, a bacterium common among many insects and harmless to humans. Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, which can transmit dengue, do not usually carry this bacterium. Wolbachia significantly reduces mosquitoes’ ability to transmit certain viruses. Females pass the bacterium on to their offspring. Therefore, after a sufficient number of such mosquitoes — males and females — are released, Wolbachia can gradually become established in the local population. Field trials in Indonesia and other countries have already shown that this strategy can noticeably reduce the number of diagnosed dengue cases. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram . Blood tests of participants In Belo Horizonte, researchers did not limit themselves to data on confirmed diagnoses, since people with mild symptoms may not receive such a diagnosis. They analyzed participants’ blood for signs of dengue, chikungunya, or the Zika virus. Boston University global health expert David Hamer, who was not involved in the study, called the results encouraging. In his view, combining this approach with other measures to combat mosquito-borne diseases could substantially reduce the spread of dengue. The study was presented amid a major dengue outbreak in the U.S. state of Florida. As of Friday, state officials had recorded more than 650 cases of local transmission, about three quarters of them in Hillsborough County, where Tampa is located. Read us on Download our app
